extracted.intended_audience: comedy writers, humor researchers, and general readers interested in joke structure
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and theoretical criteria for producing and analyzing punch lines (the final, laughter-provoking element of jokes) including linguistic, cognitive, prosodic, and structural considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punch line (definition and role)
rubrics_metrics.description: A punch line concludes a joke; it is intended to make people laugh. It is the third and final part of the typical joke structure, following the introductory framing of the joke and the narrative which sets up the punch line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example structure: framing 'A man walks into a bar...', narrative 'he hurts his head', punch line 'It was an iron bar!'. In a broader sense, 'punch line' can also refer to the unexpected and funny conclusion of any performance, situation or story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script-based semantic pivot (Raskin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is evoked when a trigger contained in the punch line causes the audience to abruptly shift its understanding of the story from the primary (more obvious) interpretation to a secondary, opposing interpretation; the punch line is 'the pivot on which the joke text turns' signalling the script shift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the humor to work the two interpretations (scripts) need to be both compatible with the joke text and opposite or incompatible with each other. (Original framing from Victor Raskin's script-based semantic theory of humor.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage incongruity: perception and resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruity alone is insufficient; humor appreciation involves two stages — discovery (perception) of an incongruity followed by a resolution of that incongruity. Resolution generates laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomas R. Shultz expands Raskin's account by emphasizing that resolution (not just the presence of incongruity) is necessary for the joke to be felicitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosodic features are unreliable indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Folk theories claim punch lines are delivered louder, at a higher pitch, or with a dramatic pause, but laboratory studies find none of these changes are employed at a statistically significant level in production of humorous narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pitch and loudness of the punch line are comparable to those of the ending of any narrative, humorous or not; do not treat prosodic 'markers' as necessary conditions for a successful punch line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-jokes and shaggy dog stories (deliberate absence or anticlimax)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shaggy dog stories are long-winded anti-jokes in which the punch line is deliberately anticlimactic; nonsense jokes have a surprising or incongruous punch line that provides no resolution or only a partial, unsatisfactory resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The humor in these forms lies in fooling the audience into expecting a typical punch line and making the audience itself the butt of the joke. Example: 'No soap radio' — anticipated resolution is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jab lines (humor embedded within the narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'jab line' designates humor within the body of a text, as opposed to the punch line which is always placed at the end. Jab lines are semantically identical to punch lines but can be positioned anywhere within the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jab lines are fully integrated in the narrative and do not disrupt flow because they are either indispensable to plot/text development or not antagonistic to it. Useful when analyzing longer humorous texts (novels, plays, sitcoms) where multiple humorous elements occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part (AAB) structure / rule of three
rubrics_metrics.description: Felicitous jokes are often formatted in an AAB structure (or A-A-A' triad): a set of three where the first two items share an attribute and the third deviates; the third item (B) is the punch line (the deviation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under these conditions the punch line is the deviation; jokes following AAB are consistently rated as funnier than AB or AAAB counterparts. Example (Rozin): two similar escape incidents followed by a deviating third that serves as the punch line. Classic genre example: 'Englishman, Irishman and Scotsman' jokes. See also the 'rule of three' in writing.
